title: Dolphins
objective: After this level you can describe how dolphins hunt and communicate.
summary: Light fades fast in the sea, but sound races through it. Dolphins read echoes to find prey, call each other by signature whistles and herd fish schools as a team.

cards.headline: In the sea, light fades fast. Sound doesn't.
cards.body: Remember Level 8: a few meters down the reds are gone, and below 1,000 m there's no sunlight at all. Dolphins solved the problem of a dim world by hunting and talking with sound.

cards.headline: A world built for sound
cards.body: Sound travels about 1,500 m per second in seawater, over four times faster than the roughly 340 m per second it manages in air. It also carries much farther in the sea. So underwater, your eyes are the weak sense and your ears are the strong one. The ocean is dim, but it is never quiet.

cards.headline: Seeing with echoes
cards.body: Dolphins use echolocation to fill in what they can't see. They send out sounds, focus them with the melon (that big rounded forehead) and read the echoes that bounce back. NOAA says a dolphin can interpret echolocation signals from about half a mile (roughly 800 m) away. It's a flashlight made of sound, and it works in the dark.
cards.callout: Send a sound · catch the echo · picture the fish

cards.headline: Names and teamwork
cards.body: Sound is also how dolphins keep in touch. Each bottlenose dolphin develops its own signature whistle, a call that works like a name. They hunt as a team, too. Remember the schools of Level 44? Bottlenose dolphins herd fish into tight groups, then take turns charging through to feed. They may even trap a school against a sandbar or seawall. The fish's crowd trick meets a crowd with a plan.

cards.headline: Dolphins: heard
learned: Sound is over four times faster in seawater than in air
Echolocation: send a sound, read the echo
Each bottlenose dolphin has a name-like whistle
Teams herd fish schools and take turns feeding

questions.prompt: What is a bottlenose dolphin's signature whistle?

options.label: A warning call that means a shark is near
options.rationale: It identifies the dolphin, like a name.

options.label: The click it uses to find fish by echo
options.rationale: That's echolocation, not the signature whistle.

options.label: A song all dolphins in a pod share
Its own distinctive call, which works like a name

questions.explanation: Each bottlenose dolphin develops its own signature whistle, a distinctive call that works like a name.

questions.prompt: Why does hunting by echolocation suit dolphins so well in the sea?

options.label: Sound travels fast and far in seawater, even where light fails
Dolphins have poor eyes and can't see at all
options.rationale: Echolocation fills gaps; it doesn't replace eyes.

options.label: Fish give off their own sounds for dolphins to hear
options.rationale: Dolphins read echoes of their own sounds.

options.label: Sound travels more slowly in water, so echoes last longer
options.rationale: Sound is over four times faster in seawater.

questions.explanation: Light fades quickly underwater, but sound travels over four times faster than in air and much farther, so echoes paint a picture in the dark.

questions.prompt: From Level 44, fish crowd into schools to stay safe. How do bottlenose dolphins turn that crowd against them?

options.label: They wait for the school to fall asleep
options.rationale: They hunt actively, as a team.

options.label: They herd the fish tight and take turns charging
They chase single fish that leave the school
options.rationale: They go after the whole school, as a team.

options.label: They whistle to scatter the school apart
options.rationale: They herd fish together, not apart.

questions.explanation: Bottlenose dolphins work together to herd fish into tight groups, then take turns charging through the school to feed.
